newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Trade panel said set to fault EU on hormone ban.
newsitem.headline: Trade panel said set to fault EU on hormone ban.

text.p: A World Trade Organisation (WTO) panel is expected to issue an interim report this week backing a U.S. complaint against the European Union's ban on imports of hormone-treated beef, diplomats said on Tuesday.
The strictly confidential report by the three-member neutral panel in the decade-old dispute is likely to be sent to the two powers on Wednesday, according to the diplomats.
"I think there can be little doubt that it will go against the EU," said one envoy whose country is not involved in the dispute.
"Purely on a legal basis, I don't think the EU has a leg to stand on, and they know it," another said.
But, under the WTO's step-by-step dispute settlement procedure, it could still be many months before a final ruling is approved by the current 131 members of the trade body.
The two parties will have a month to return their comments on the interim report, and only then will the panel issue its formal ruling.
Whichever way the ruling goes, an appeal is likely and this could extend the process to near the end of the year.

If the ruling goes against the Brussels-headquartered EU, it would almost certainly mean that the 15-nation bloc would lose an identical dispute with Canada in which the same three-man panel is preparing a report likely to be issued in August.

But in the past EU officials have indicated that, because of the strength of EU public opinion against the use of hormones in food processing, Brussels would prefer to pay compensation rather than drop the ban.
There was no immediate comment from U.S. officials on what they expected from the interim report, contents of which are likely to leak first in Washington or Brussels.

But, throughout the dispute, which began in 1988 when the EU implemented a ban on imports of meat treated with growth hormones, Washington has argued it is on strong ground because there was no scientific basis for the ban.
The United States has the backing of Australia, New Zealand and Norway in the dispute.
Washington first brought the dispute to the WTO's predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade or GATT, in 1987, just over a year after the original EU decision to bring in the ban.
But under the GATT's less tough dispute settlement rules, movement was blocked and in 1989 the United States slapped 10 per cent duties on a range of EU products in retaliation.
Two years ago, the EU launched a WTO process against these measures. But they were dropped when Washington started its case in the WTO and the EU then suspended its own complaint.
